The z-score tells you how many standard deviations away from the mean an individual data point is in a normally distributed dataset. It measures the number of standard deviations that separate the data point from the mean, which provides insight into its relative position within the dataset.

A z-score of 0 means that the data point is equal to the mean. A positive z-score indicates that the data point is above the mean, while a negative z-score indicates that it's below the mean.

The magnitude of the z-score (i.e., its absolute value) tells you how unusual or extreme the data point is. A z-score close to 0 (between -1 and 1) indicates that the data point is relatively common or typical, as it's within one standard deviation of the mean. A z-score greater than 1 or less than -1 indicates that the data point is less common or more extreme.

For example, in a normally distributed dataset, about 68% of data points will have a z-score between -1 and 1, about 95% will have a z-score between -2 and 2, and about 99.7% will have a z-score between -3 and 3. Z-scores beyond -3 or 3 are typically considered extreme or outliers. 

In the context of the exam score dataset, the z-score of 2.17 for an exam score of 95 indicates that this score is significantly above the mean (more than 2 standard deviations away), suggesting that it's an exceptionally high score.

T(1, 0) = (a, c)
T(0, 1) = (b, d)

where (a, c) and (b, d) are the images of the basis vectors under the transformation. These vectors are the columns of the matrix representation of T.

The matrix representation of T is then:

T = | a  b |

= x(a, c) + y(b, d)
